wodscience_videos.t: How Alyssa McElheny Did 350 Unbroken Wall Balls
wodscience_videos.s: I mean what can I say more, Alyssa Mcelheny did 350 wall balls unbroken. We had the opportunity to test her physiology and biomechanics at adidas HQ. Using this data I break down why her special physiology allows here to move for 11+ min straight at a wall ball cycling rate of 31 reps per minute. A sciency one, hope you enjoy.
c: The next step in testing hyrox athletes
How could Alyssa do 350 wall balls unbroken? (physiology)
Want to do this test yourself (wodmotions)

wodscience_videos.t: How Fit Are HYROX Athletes, Actually? (We Built the Ultimate Test)
wodscience_videos.s: A project in the making for two years! In this video I guide you through a HYROX specific test I built with the team of WODMotions. Instead of doing only running or rowing we mimic a traditional ramp test to exhaustion using functional movements, yes the ones that are used in hyrox fitness racing. Wall-balls, burpees and running. I will show you the results of the test, the fully fledged report and what the data could mean for your training and coaching services. A lot of state of the art info is shared in this video. I hope you enjoy!
c: You can do the test yourself!

wodscience_videos.t: Why Sprints Improve Endurance Without Building More Mitochondria
wodscience_videos.s: Want to train harder, stay injury-free, and actually enjoy it? Sprinting increases endurance capacity, including VO2max. That is interesting, because exercise intensity is not directly related to how much mitochondria you build within your muscle (mitochondrial biogenesis). So where are those benefits from sprinting coming from? Well, in this video I breakdown a fascinating & recent paper that investigates exactly that: the divergent response of mitochondrial adaptations to 1. moderate intensity continuous exercise and 2. sprinting. A bit of a more sciency video, hope you enjoy! Some references I recommend reading: ** Botella J et al., https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41326383/ ** All the wor
c: Study set-up: continuous vs. sprint exercise
The long-term effects on mitochondria of endurance vs sprint training

wodscience_videos.t: It’s NOT Strength You Lose Fastest With Age
wodscience_videos.s: Want to train harder, stay injury-free, and actually enjoy it? “You gotta lift weights to stay healthy and strong.” That’s the message you’ll hear from many of the biggest health and fitness podcasts, and it’s also reflected in the recommendations from the World Health Organization. And it’s good advice. But in this video, I make the case that there is another physical quality we should be paying much more attention to as we age: POWER. The ability to produce force quickly. To move fast, against moderate loads. In this video, I break down some of the most important research on muscle power and aging, why power declines even faster than strength, and why this matters for maintaining physical

wodscience_videos.t: The Real Reason VO₂max Declines With Age — And Why It Changes How You Should Train
wodscience_videos.s: Want to train harder, stay injury-free, and actually enjoy it? Maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max), one of the best markers of cardiorespiratory fitness, unfortunately declines with age. Whether you're an endurance athlete or someone with a desk job, some degree of decline seems inevitable. But why does it happen? In this video, I discuss a fascinating new paper in which the authors modeled data from 25+ previous studies to understand what actually drives the age-related decline in VO₂max. Is it mainly the heart and our ability to deliver oxygen, or does the problem increasingly lie within the muscles and their ability to extract and use oxygen? I found the results super interesting when I first

wodscience_videos.t: Protein Isn’t Your #1 Recovery Nutrient. Carbs are.
wodscience_videos.s: Want to train harder, stay injury-free, and actually enjoy it? We get bombarded with high-protein foods these days, it’s just phenomenal. Well in this video I discuss the scientific data on macronutrients and their impact on acute recovery. Based on my own experiments (see paper below) and those of colleagues I make the case that carbs are actually much more important than protein when it comes to recovery from hard exercise within let’s say 24h. Some references I recommend reading: My paper: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36252815/ Podlogar narrative review: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40221559/ PDF with all nutritional recommendations for recovery: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/52nc7

wodscience_videos.t: HIIT Gets You Fit Fast – Here's What to Do Next

wodscience_videos.s: Here are some things we created to level-up your coaching and training: The CrossFit methodology is built on high-intensity. “Be impressed by intensity, not by volume” – famous words by CrossFit founder Greg Glassman. This is why we launched the ZONE 2 Project for CrossFit three months ago. wodscience_videos.t: Two Tips to Stay Injury-Free in CrossFit (according to science)
wodscience_videos.s: Injuries in high-intensity sports, such as CrossFit, are relatively common. But just how common are they, and how do the odds compare to those in other sports? In this video, I discuss a new study on injuries in CrossFit. German researchers surveyed over 300 athletes of various ages and skill levels about their injury rates during CrossFit training. The data revealed that barbell exercises, box jumps, and pull-ups were most commonly associated with injuries among CrossFit participants. Additionally, research by Miwais Mehrab and colleagues indicates that a sudden increase in training load is the most significant factor in causing injuries in high-intensity sports.

In this video you will find out how to determine YOUR optimal resting time using the newest wearable technology (Near Infrared Spectroscopy, NIRS). Burpee 7 min (+9%) e Karen 150 wall balls (+15%) só melhoraram no grupo academia; 5 km (+4,6%) só no grupo corrida.

wodscience_resumos.t: Dose mínima de força para HYROX
p: Volume semanal (séries por grupo muscular) é o fator nº 1; frequência importa pouco quando o volume é igual.
Bickel 2011: depois de 16 semanas de força, 1/9 do volume (1 série/grupo, 1x/semana) manteve a massa muscular por 32 semanas.
Quem vem da força (CrossFit): 1 sessão pesada/semana, 4-8 séries de perna, carga alta, 1-3 reps na reserva — e jogar o resto do tempo em condicionamento.
Quem vem do endurance: base com 2-3 sessões/semana, 10-15 séries de perna, carga moderada, 4-5 RIR; fase específica 2x/semana, 8-12 séries a 70-85% 1RM, 1-3 RIR.
Para Hyrox o objetivo é força, não hipertrofia; ficar grande demais atrapalha.
Periodize em blocos: foque um aspecto por 8-12 semanas e mantenha os outros.
Depois de deadlift + lunges, o mesmo ritmo de corrida custou +12,5% de O2 num crossfiteiro e +4,4% num atleta Elite 15 de Hyrox.
Durante as estações o RER passou de 1,2: forte componente anaeróbio, mesmo com VO2 igual ao da corrida.
Causas: redistribuição de sangue para os músculos grandes, acidose local (mitocôndria menos eficiente) e pior extração de O2.
Primeiro um bloco longo só de corrida; corrida comprometida só depois, mais perto da prova.
Educativos de corrida, pliometria e força melhoram a economia de corrida (rigidez do tendão e eficiência neuromuscular).
Meta-análise: pequena interferência na força de perna em homens; nenhuma no VO2máx.
Com volume igualado, força + bike melhorou mais o VO2pico do que força + circuito de barra (que não melhorou o VO2).
Regra 1: separar força de endurance leve/moderado (dias diferentes ou ≥6 h).
Regra 2: maximizar o volume/carga semanal possível na agenda do atleta.
Regra 3: intervalado intenso combina melhor com força no mesmo dia do que endurance moderado.
Para atleta amador, juntar no mesmo treino é aceitável; separar importa mais para quem busca elite.
Limiar = maior intensidade com lactato estável (MLSS); pode ser estimado por lactato, NIRS, FTP (~95% de 20 min), FC (~88-93% FCmáx) ou PSE 6-7/10.
Um Elite 15 de Hyrox corria a prova (3:30-3:40/km) praticamente na velocidade do limiar (~17,4 km/h).
Estudo de 9 semanas em atletas treinados: polarizado +10% VO2máx, HIIT +5%, só limiar não melhorou.
Erro comum no funcional: todo AMRAP/for time acaba acima do limiar; varie a intensidade na semana (sprint, Z2, limiar, específico).
Sugestão: duplo limiar — manhã 4×7 min no limiar (corrida/erg); tarde um EMOM funcional a PSE 7 (ex.: sled, pull-up, wall ball) segurando ritmo sustentável.
